Swiss chocolate company Camille Bloch has not been spared by the fall in chocolate consumption. Its director, Daniel Bloch, attributes this decline to this summer’s heatwave.
“Compared with last year, which wasn’t a great year to begin with, we recorded a further decline in 2026 of around 10%,” said Bloch in an interview with RJB, published on Tuesday in the JdJ.
Several factors are at play, such as the price of chocolate, the general consumer climate and the heat, as people eat less chocolate when it is hot.

Swiss chocolate is part of the country’s identity. But its global success owes as much to clever marketing as to taste and quality.
Camille Bloch has no intention of resorting to permanent promotions. “In the long term, this could damage the reputation of our brands and our profit margins,” said Bloch. The company intends to improve efficiency and keep costs under control.
“There is a decline, but not a general collapse. That said, it has been going on for some time. So we need to adapt,” said Bloch, who believes it is essential to continue innovating. Faced with the contraction of the Swiss market, the chocolate maker is seeking further growth abroad, particularly in the Caucasus markets.
The company is now hoping for a turnaround. “We hope that demand will pick up again as temperatures drop and the festive season approaches,” said Bloch.
The manufacturer believes that the end of the year will be a crucial period for seeing whether this recovery materialises and to what extent it can offset this summer’s slowdown.

A strong El Nino is expected to shorten southern Vietnam's 2026 rainy season and reduce rainfall, with temperatures in Ho Chi Minh City and surrounding areas potentially exceeding 38°C during the peak dry season in 2027.
According to the Southern Regional Hydrometeorological Station, weather patterns across southern Vietnam are expected to undergo significant changes in the final months of 2026 and early 2027 under the influence of El Nino.
Rainy season to end early as rainfall declines
Forecasters predict that the rainy season in southern Vietnam could end around 10-15 days earlier than the long-term average, likely during the first half of November 2026.
In November, the region is expected to experience approximately 7-15 rainy days. This figure could decline to 4-10 days in December, with only 2-7 days of scattered rainfall forecast for January 2027.
Total rainfall over the three-month period is expected to be 5-20% below the long-term average.
Tay Ninh, Ho Chi Minh City and Lam Dong are among the areas facing a particularly significant risk of rainfall shortages.
The decline in precipitation will not only bring an earlier end to the rainy season but also increase the risk of water shortages during the approaching dry season.
Temperatures could exceed 38°C during peak dry season
Alongside declining rainfall, temperatures across southern Vietnam are forecast to rise in the coming months.
From November 2026 to January 2027, average monthly temperatures could be 0.5-1°C above the long-term average.
However, relatively strong cold air activity is expected to prevent temperatures from rising sharply during this period.
Daily highs will generally range between 31°C and 34°C, although some days could see temperatures climb above 35°C.
From February to April 2027, southern Vietnam will enter the peak of its dry season.
Unseasonal rainfall is expected to become extremely rare, while sunshine will intensify and hot weather will become more frequent.
Notably, March and April 2027 could bring prolonged periods of intense heat, with temperatures commonly reaching 35-38°C and potentially exceeding 38°C in some areas.
The rainfall and temperature forecasts for the coming months are intended to help residents and authorities prepare appropriate response measures, adjust production activities and manage water resources more effectively.
Early planning will be essential to limiting the adverse impacts of the 2026-2027 dry season.

In high-stakes business environments, executive teams frequently struggle to maintain organizational momentum without burning out their staff. Leaders often trigger an emergency response only when deadlines loom or performance metrics fall behind, creating counterproductive stress across departments.
On the latest episode of Lessons in Leadership, Leadership Expert Dave Anderson examines the 14th commandment of his 15 Commandments for Organizational Peak Performance, focusing on how leaders can establish a continuous rhythm of urgency through direct activity management.
According to Anderson, when organizations delay operational intensity until the end of a month or quarter, the resulting pressure often degrades performance rather than improving it. He believes that turning urgency on and off creates a volatile environment that leads to operational mistakes.
"I just love the term red alert. To me, it evokes urgency, focus, unity... The problem is we often don't go on red alert in many organizations until time is running out, until we're behind, the month is winding down. Now we've got urgency, but it's unhealthy. We're pressing, we're stressing, and people are tense, and now they're making mistakes, worsening things."
To avoid reactive crisis management, Anderson emphasizes making urgency a foundational rhythm embedded in daily company culture.
Essential activities over final outcomes
Achieving sustained organizational momentum requires a shift in managerial focus. Rather than attempting to control end results directly, leaders must manage the daily execution of key operational behaviors.
By identifying essential daily tasks and holding employees accountable for completing them, leaders create a predictable operational cadence.
Anderson added that daily urgency requires identifying essential activities and holding people accountable the next day for completing them. This creates a consistent accountability rhythm that fosters urgency, strengthens habits, sustains energy, and improves results. He urged the team to remain on high alert.
